messages.subject: Comments on Command Refactor
parts:
If people have a minute can you check out the current progress at
feature/issue-1361-writer_callback? This branch introduces a
writer callback and then refactors a ton of services to use the
callback. Some of that refactoring addresses a bunch of
outstanding issues and substantially pushes command towards
the spec outlined at https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-API-Refactor.

If people are cool with it I’ll proceed to the next step, which involves
pushing the writer callback all the way through the sampling and
optimization codes and then updating an incredibly large number of
tests (not to mention adding a bunch of new ones).

-Betancourt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Comments on Command Refactor
parts:
I did some major edits on the services and interface proposal:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-API-Refactor

I tried to flesh out the missing arguments to the command
service function, added a discussion of templating vs.
abstract base classes for the callback option, and added
a discussion of just replacing everything with JSON or
Protocol Buffers. I tried to lay out more of what each
component needs as well as discussing some pros and cons
as I see them without trying to editorialize my own opinions.

My own opinion is that we should go the callback route.
I think the pros outweigh the cons, unless the pain to
Allen and Jiqiang of writing C++ is so great as to outweigh
the other benefits.

Feel free to continue editing --- I'm sure I missed some of
the pros and cons.

We need to dive one level deeper and start fleshing out what
each of the elements is going to be. I think I'll go and drop
in the CmdStan config skeletons, which I think show what's going
on.

This also brings up the issue of whether the interfaces provide
a monolithic god-object for config and single function, or whether they
break things down more modularly. I'm in favor of smaller functions,
which is why I documented CmdStan as I did, whereas I believe Michael's
in favor of the god-object approach, which is why the config is
implemented as it is. So the implementation/interface decisions
can go their own way.

- Bob

interfaces use command nothing in this branch has a huge

the whole point of a unified UX is that the interfaces _don’t_
get to do whatever they want. We’re getting dangerously
close to every interface being completely independent, and
once that happens we lose a tremendous potential for Stan.

messages.author: 512610f4917ceaf3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Comments on Command Refactor
parts:
Hi,

Yes, Bob's summary is very useful.

As far as Julia and today’s Stan.jl are concerned, for Julia 0.3.x Allen’s earlier comment about following R and Python without C++ is correct. As alternatives folks can also fall back to RCall.jl and/or PyCall.jl.

Once Julia 0.4 + Cxx.jl are in general use (2nd half of this year?) I’ll reconsider if 1) I am convinced I don’t end up in the C++/Rtools version struggles across the 3 platforms and 2) there are clear advantages in using the C++ APIs.

As far as item 1) is concerned, my goal remains to install Stan through build.jl when installing Stan.jl. As far as item 2) is concerned, I do not consider ’shelling out’ CmdStan in Julia’s case a mistake because it keeps using Make simple (and thus averts extra compilations), it gives parallel chains almost for free and as Bob also mentioned I’ve not seen a case yet where i/o was a real bottleneck.

Either way, I’m on board with a callback (API) approach. From the Julia user (interface) point of view, Stan.jl attempts to bring Stan to Julia, not vice versa. Like input data pre-processing, I probably prefer ‘common’ configuration (e.g. dictionary based) and posterior tools for Julia/JuliaStats (today’s Stan.jl is leaning heavily on Mamba.jl).

As I am going to work on on-line help stuff for Stan.jl next week I’ll certainly keep this discussion in mind.

Regards,
Rob

Cheers,
Marcus

This is, by the way, the reason I originally used vector<double> instead
of Eigen --- it's just more portable to other interfaces.

Yes, memory is contiguous for vector<double>, but not vector<vector<double> >.

Marcus is absolutely right that there's no way to create a vector<double> from
a double* without copying, even in C++11, because vector<double> wants to manage
the memory. That's the main advantage of using it over a double* (other than
that you also don't have to keep passing lengths around). See:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/vector/vector/vector/

Yes, we can copy a vector<double> to another without a deep copy using move
semantics in C++11. Or swap as Rob points out.

To avoid copying a vector<double>, can't we pass by reference, or by
pointer as a last resort? Or we can manage memory using a vector<double>
and pass a reference to the memory, but this is dangerous, as resizing
can cause the contents to move. That is, a vector<double> is guaranteed
to have contiguous memory at any given time, but that location is just
a handle, not a hard reference, so it may move.

We can't create a MatrixXd in Eigen without a copy, but we can use
the Map<MatrixXd> expression template to do the copy lazily or not
at all depending on how it's used.

parts:
> On Apr 2, 2015, at 12:04 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>
> If it's only a vector<double> you can use Map<MatrixXd> to map it onto
> an Eigen matrix without a copy.

Map<MatrixXd> is an expression template that wraps raw data.
As soon as it's assigned, there's a copy implicated. So if you do this:

Map<MatrixXd> y(...);
MatrixXd m <- y;

you get a copy. If you just use it in something like an addition,
you can sometimes avoid the copy.

> It's the vector<vector<double>> that's
> the problem (and a big one, since that's how RStan and PyStan hold their
> chains).
OK --- that decisions on the RStan and PyStan side.

> Is there any C++11 way to create a vector<vector<double>> that is
> contiguous?

No. A vector<double> manages its memory independently on the heap.

You need to use an array. Or use the Boost Array package to do it
more generally.

> Can we use an std::array or something? If there was a way to
> do this cleanly, RStan and PyStan could use Stan's ess and rhat
> routines.

std::array is C++11, I'm afraid. It also doesn't do anything for you
other than template out the size so the size is static, which you
don't want.

I don't see anything for you other than to malloc your own 2D array
structure. I'd suggest doing it following std::vector so it uses
the RAII pattern in C++ and thus will ensure memory safety.

- Bob
